title: Instruction tuning and RLHF
text:
CHAPTER 19. LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS
SECTION 19.1. INSTRUCTION TUNING AND RLHF

A pretrained language model like GPT-3 (Section 18.3) is a powerful text predictor, but not a helpful assistant. Ask it "Explain the moon landing to a six-year-old" and it might continue with more questions in the same style, as if completing a list of exam prompts, because that is a plausible continuation of internet text. It may also produce falsehoods, toxic language or harmful instructions, all of which occur in its training data. Turning a predictor into an assistant that follows instructions and behaves acceptably required two further training stages: instruction tuning (supervised fine-tuning on examples of good responses) and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). These methods, developed between 2017 and 2022, were the technical difference between GPT-3 and ChatGPT (Section 19.2).

1. The alignment problem in miniature

The pretraining objective, predicting the next token of internet text, is not the same as what users want: helpful, honest and harmless answers. In "Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback" (Long Ouyang and colleagues, OpenAI, March 2022), the authors put it this way: making language models bigger does not inherently make them better at following a user's intent; such models are "not aligned with their users." The general problem of making AI systems pursue the goals their designers and users intend is called alignment (Section 20.2). Instruction tuning and RLHF are the first practical, widely deployed alignment methods.

2. Instruction tuning

The simplest fix is supervised fine-tuning (SFT): collect examples of instructions paired with good responses and continue training the model on them with the ordinary next-token loss (computed on the response tokens).

Several 2021-2022 papers showed that fine-tuning on many tasks phrased as natural language instructions makes models much better at following new instructions they have never seen:

  - FLAN (Jason Wei and colleagues, Google, September 2021) took a 137-billion-parameter pretrained model and instruction-tuned it on over 60 NLP datasets rewritten with instruction templates ("Is the sentiment of this review positive or negative?"). On unseen task types, it surpassed zero-shot 175B GPT-3 on 20 of 25 tasks evaluated. Ablations showed that the benefit grew with the number of tasks and with model size; small models could even get worse.
  - T0 (Victor Sanh and colleagues, BigScience, October 2021) showed similar zero-shot generalization with a multitask prompted training mixture for an 11-billion-parameter T5 model.
  - Flan-PaLM and Flan-T5 (Hyung Won Chung and colleagues, October 2022) scaled instruction tuning to about 1,800 tasks and included chain-of-thought examples (Section 19.3).

Instruction tuning teaches the format of being an assistant: respond to the request, rather than continuing the text. But supervised examples have limits. Writing excellent demonstrations is slow and expensive, and the model learns to imitate the demonstrations, including their limitations, without learning which of two possible answers people prefer. Comparing answers is much easier for people than writing perfect ones, which is the idea behind RLHF.

3. Learning from human preferences

Paul Christiano, Jan Leike, Tom Brown, Miljan Martic, Shane Legg and Dario Amodei (OpenAI and DeepMind, "Deep reinforcement learning from human preferences," June 2017) showed that an RL agent (Section 16.4) can learn complex behavior without a reward function, from human comparisons between pairs of short video clips of its behavior. A reward model was trained to predict which clip the human would prefer, and the agent was trained with RL to maximize the predicted reward. Feedback was needed on less than one percent of the agent's interactions; a simulated robot learned to do a backflip with about an hour of human time.

The comparison model is the Bradley-Terry model (Ralph Bradley and Milton Terry, 1952), originally for ranking players from paired comparisons. If a reward model r assigns scalar scores to outputs, the probability that output A is preferred to B is

    P(A preferred to B) = s( r(A) - r(B) )

where s is the sigmoid. Training minimizes the negative log-likelihood of the observed human preferences:

    loss = - log s( r(chosen) - r(rejected) )

Example: if r(chosen) - r(rejected) = 1.5, the model assigns s(1.5), about 0.82, to the observed preference, and the loss is about 0.20. If the difference were -1.5 (the model scored the rejected answer higher), the loss would be about 1.70, and gradient descent pushes the scores apart in the right direction. Only differences matter, so reward models are trained on comparisons, not absolute ratings.

Nisan Stiennon and colleagues (OpenAI, "Learning to summarize from human feedback," September 2020) applied this to language: a model fine-tuned with RL against a reward model trained on human comparisons of summaries produced summaries that people preferred to those of a model trained only with supervised learning, and even to the human-written reference summaries in the dataset.

4. InstructGPT: the three-step recipe

Ouyang and colleagues (March 2022) applied the method to GPT-3, using prompts submitted to the OpenAI API (and others written by labelers), and a team of about 40 contractors hired through Upwork and Scale AI. The procedure, which became the standard recipe:

  Step 1, supervised fine-tuning: labelers wrote demonstrations of desired responses; GPT-3 was fine-tuned on them (about 13,000 training prompts).

  Step 2, reward model: for each prompt, several model outputs were sampled and labelers ranked them; a reward model (initialized from a language model, with a scalar output head) was trained on the comparisons with the Bradley-Terry loss (about 33,000 training prompts, each with several ranked outputs).

  Step 3, reinforcement learning: the SFT model was fine-tuned with PPO (proximal policy optimization; John Schulman and colleagues, 2017) to maximize the reward model's score on new prompts (about 31,000 prompts), with a penalty for moving too far from the SFT model:

    objective = E[ r(x, y) ] - beta * KL( pi_RL(y | x) || pi_SFT(y | x) )

    where x is the prompt, y the response, pi the policies, and KL the Kullback-Leibler divergence.

The KL penalty is essential. A reward model is only an approximation of human judgment, and a policy optimized hard against it will find outputs that score highly but are not actually good (reward hacking, "Goodhart's law": when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure). Keeping the policy close to the SFT model limits this. The final InstructGPT version also mixed in pretraining gradients (called PPO-ptx) to reduce performance losses on standard NLP benchmarks, which the authors called an "alignment tax."

Results: in human evaluations on the API prompt distribution, outputs from the 1.3-billion-parameter InstructGPT model were preferred to those of the 175-billion-parameter GPT-3, despite having more than 100 times fewer parameters. InstructGPT also improved truthfulness and reduced toxic output, with minimal regressions on public benchmarks, though it still made simple mistakes. OpenAI made InstructGPT models the default in its API in early 2022, and the same approach, applied to a model tuned for dialogue, produced ChatGPT in November 2022.

Whose preferences? The paper was explicit that the model was aligned to the preferences of a specific group of labelers, following instructions written by OpenAI researchers, for the kinds of prompts API customers sent, not to some universal standard of human values. This remains a basic issue in alignment work.

5. Variations: helpful, harmless and constitutional

  - Anthropic's "Training a Helpful and Harmless Assistant with RLHF" (Yuntao Bai and colleagues, April 2022) studied the tension between helpfulness and harmlessness (a model can be made "safe" by refusing everything, which is useless) and trained preference models on both.
  - Constitutional AI (Bai and colleagues, Anthropic, December 2022) reduced dependence on human labels for harmlessness. The only human oversight is a list of written principles (the "constitution"). In a supervised phase, the model critiques and revises its own responses according to the principles; in an RL phase, a model judges which of two responses better follows the principles, and these AI preferences train the reward model, "RL from AI feedback" (RLAIF). The paper reported a harmless but non-evasive assistant that explains its objections to harmful requests rather than simply refusing.
  - Direct Preference Optimization (DPO; Rafael Rafailov, Archit Sharma, Eric Mitchell, Stefano Ermon, Christopher Manning and Chelsea Finn, Stanford, May 2023) showed that the KL-regularized RLHF objective has a closed-form optimal policy, which allows the reward model to be eliminated: the policy is trained directly on preference pairs with a simple classification-style loss,

        loss = - log s( beta * [ log (pi(y_w|x)/pi_ref(y_w|x)) - log (pi(y_l|x)/pi_ref(y_l|x)) ] )

    where y_w is the preferred and y_l the rejected response and pi_ref the reference (SFT) model. DPO is simpler and more stable than PPO and became widely used, especially for open models.
  - Parameter-efficient fine-tuning, such as LoRA (Edward Hu and colleagues, Microsoft, 2021), which trains small low-rank update matrices (W + B A, with B and A of rank r much smaller than the layer width) instead of all weights, made instruction tuning of large open models affordable on a single GPU.

6. What RLHF does and does not do

Effects widely observed:

  - Models follow instructions, keep to the requested format, and decline some harmful requests.
  - Answers become longer and more confident; reward models often favor length and a confident tone, a form of reward hacking that must be controlled.
  - "Sycophancy": models trained on human approval tend to agree with the user's stated views or praise their work, because people tend to rate agreement highly.
  - Calibration (whether stated confidence matches accuracy) can get worse after RLHF; the GPT-4 technical report showed such a reduction for its model.
  - Safety training can be bypassed with "jailbreak" prompts, which shows that it modifies behavior on typical inputs rather than removing underlying capabilities.

Most researchers view RLHF as shaping and eliciting abilities that pretraining created, rather than adding new knowledge. In 2024-2026, reinforcement learning moved beyond human preferences to verifiable rewards, such as whether a math answer is correct or code passes its tests, which produced the reasoning models of Section 19.3.

7. Summary

  - Pretrained language models predict text but do not reliably follow instructions or avoid harm; alignment training addresses this.
  - Instruction tuning (FLAN, T0, Flan-PaLM, 2021-2022) fine-tunes on many tasks phrased as instructions and improves zero-shot generalization, especially in large models.
  - RLHF (Christiano and colleagues, 2017; Stiennon and colleagues, 2020) trains a reward model on human comparisons with the Bradley-Terry loss, then optimizes the policy with RL.
  - InstructGPT (Ouyang and colleagues, March 2022): SFT, reward model, PPO with a KL penalty; a 1.3B model was preferred to 175B GPT-3.
  - Constitutional AI and RLAIF (Anthropic, 2022), DPO (2023) and LoRA simplified or extended the recipe.
  - RLHF has known side effects: reward hacking, length bias, sycophancy and jailbreak vulnerability.
